metadata.title: The Bottleneck Moved.

metadata.color_semantics: Fidelity claude palette throughout. ONE terracotta #D97757 event per beat — it marks the cost that did NOT fall (attention/trust) in every body beat, so the accent carries the argument rather than decorating it.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, with RESULT lines), B03 (ask micro-beat of the one ask->result pair), B07 (verdict artifact), B08 (handoff), B09 (outro). Every other beat illustrates its concept with a registered rhetorical pattern from deckPatterns.tsx — no two consecutive beats share a scheme. HONESTY: this reel argues from a stated model and asserts NO measured external figures; every magnitude on screen is an explicitly-labelled ordinal ranking (see FACTCHECK.md).

beats.narration_text: Every marketing team just got a machine that writes faster than they can publish. This is Yatra, in for Bear. So why isn't anyone's reach going up? Today — the part of marketing AI made free, and the part it never touched.

show.event: Cream page, spark mark, serif greeting 'Merhaba, Yatra' settles above the composer
The ask types itself into the composer, character by character
Terracotta send button arms — the ONE accent event of the beat
Running indicator: 'separating the two costs…'
Three result lines stagger in — the ask lands ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW)

props.command: My team adopted AI across marketing this year. Output is up roughly 5x and reach is flat. Separate the costs for me: which parts of marketing did AI actually make cheaper, which parts did it leave exactly where they were, and which part are we now over-investing in because it got cheap?
output: cheaper: producing the asset — drafts, variants, images
unchanged: earning the attention, earning the trust
you scaled the step that was already free

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath. AI collapsed the cost of making marketing content — drafts, variants, images — effectively to zero. It did not collapse the cost of being worth someone's attention. Two costs that always moved together just came apart. Everything after this follows from that split.

beats.narration_text: So look at where the work actually sits now. Generating the draft — minutes, near free. Getting it in front of the right person — unchanged. You still buy, earn, or borrow that attention. Being believed once you're there — harder than before, because everyone got the same machine.

beats.narration_text: So I asked Claude to draw the other half — what actually happens to a piece of content after you hit publish.

props.command: Draw the attention funnel a single marketing asset passes through after it is published — published, seen, read, remembered, acted on. Label the stages honestly as an ordinal shape, not measured data, and mark which stages a faster writing tool changes.

beats.narration_text: This is the funnel AI didn't touch. Published, then seen, then read, then remembered, then acted on. Every stage sheds most of what enters it, and not one of those stages cares how fast the thing was written. Double what goes in the top, and you double the top.

A terracotta bracket sweeps the whole chain labelled 'AI changes none of these' — the ONE accent
Top of the chain doubles in width; the tail visibly does NOT move. Held ≥2s

beats.narration_text: And there's a cutoff — this is where the model could be wrong. Below some volume, more output does buy more reach; a small brand posting twice a week gains by posting five times. Above it, volume costs you — the feed learns your name means filler. If your reach keeps scaling past that point, this model doesn't fit you.

Below-threshold zone fills ink: 'more output → more reach' — verdict reads YES
The threshold line snaps in on the spoken word 'cutoff', terracotta — the ONE accent
Above-threshold zone fills: 'more output → less trust' — verdict flips to NO
Falsifier caption types beneath: 'if reach still scales here, this model is wrong for you'. Held ≥2s

beats.narration_text: So, a worked example. A team frees up twenty hours a week. Branch one: same targeting, five times the output — they're buying more of the step that was already free. Branch two: same output, twenty hours spent on who it's for and whether it's true — buying down the step that stayed expensive. The framework picks branch two.

Branch A draws down-left: '5× the output' — and the B02 cost-bars ghost in behind it, showing it feeding the ALREADY-CHEAP bar
Branch B draws down-right: '20 hrs on targeting + truth' — ghost bars show it feeding the EXPENSIVE bar, in terracotta
Resolver panel types in beneath: 'buy down the cost that did NOT fall'; branch B's path thickens. Both branches held side-by-side ≥2s

resolver.detail: Production is solved. Attention is not.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. One — AI made producing marketing content nearly free. Two — it left the cost of attention and trust exactly where it was. Three — the bottleneck moved, so optimizing production is optimizing the part that's already solved. And the honest caveat: this is a model, not a measurement. Test it on your own numbers before you reorganize a team around it.

show.event: Claude artifact page opens on the cream ground
Four verdict lines stagger in, one per spoken clause
The caveat line lands last and holds — terracotta rule beneath it, the ONE accent

artifactLines: Production cost — collapsed. Drafts, variants, images: effectively free.
Attention and trust — unchanged. No stage of the funnel cares how fast it was written.
So the bottleneck moved. Optimizing output is optimizing the solved half.
Caveat: this is a model, not a measurement. Test it against your own numbers first.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: take my last twenty marketing assets, and for each one tell me which cost it was buying down — production, distribution, or trust — then show me where my hours actually went. Run it, then grade the answer on three things. Does it sort every asset? Does it disagree with you anywhere? Does it name hours you can't account for? If it agrees with everything, you gave it too little to work with.
